lesson.label: 🧠 Brainstorming questions (Câu hỏi nên nghĩ trước buổi học)
items: Where’s your hometown, and **how often do you go back?**
What do you **miss most about your hometown** when you’re away?
Would you rather **live in a big city, by the sea or in the mountains**? Why?
How **has your hometown changed** since you were a child?

lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. The grass is always greener
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Minh, from Hà Nội, and Vy, from Quy Nhơn, are stuck in a taxi in rush-hour traffic.*
lines: We’ve moved about ten metres in fifteen minutes. **I can’t stand this traffic!**
Honestly, this city is **a concrete jungle**. Back in Quy Nhơn, I’d be home by now, probably sitting on the beach with a coconut.
**Don’t rub it in!** But come on, you love it here a little bit.
Well, the food here is amazing, and **there’s always something to do**. Whatever you’re **in the mood for**, you’re **spoilt for choice**.
Exactly. And **the career prospects** are way better. Half my friends from university moved here for work.
True, but **the daily grind** really **wears you down**. Two hours in traffic every day, breathing in all that **smog**…
**Fair point.** So what’s a normal day like back home?

**Pure bliss!** My parents’ house is **a stone’s throw from** the beach, so I **wake up to the sound of the waves**. Every morning, my mum goes to the fish market and **haggles** for **the catch of the day**.
Stop, you’re making me hungry! But don’t you get bored? I’d miss being able to go out late at night.
Haha, **that’s the only downside**. Most places close by nine. But people there have **a real sense of community**. If you’re ill, half the street **turns up** with soup.
That’s lovely. In my building, nobody even **makes eye contact** in the lift.
Has Hà Nội changed much since you were a kid?
**Beyond recognition.** The rice fields near my grandma’s house are now huge **apartment complexes**.
Same in Quy Nhơn. Since the tourists started **pouring in**, luxury resorts have been **popping up** all along the coast.
I guess **the grass is always greener**. I’d **swap** this traffic **for** a beach **any day**.

lesson.label: Tell us about your hometown
head: Purposes
Phrases
rows: **Where is it? What’s it known for?**

• ***I’m from…, a busy city / a coastal city / a small town in…***
• ***It’s about … hours from… by bus / plane.***
• ***It’s best known for… / It’s famous for…***
• ***It’s not very well-known, but…***

• ***Life there moves at a much slower / faster pace than in…***
• ***A typical day starts with… and ends with…***
• ***After work, most people…***
**What do you love? What wears you down?**

• ***What I love most about it is…***
• ***The best thing about living there is…***
• ***The daily grind / the traffic / the heat really wears you down.***
• ***The one thing I can’t stand is…***
• ***The only downside is that…***
**What are the people like? How do you feel about it?**

• ***People there are really down-to-earth / easy-going / hard-working.***
• ***There’s a real sense of community. Everyone looks out for each other.***
• ***Sometimes I feel like a stranger in my own city.***
• ***Whenever I go back, I feel completely at home.***

lesson.title: 2. Then and now
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Quân, from Sài Gòn, and Ngọc, from Đà Lạt, are friends. They’re having coffee after the long weekend.*
lines: You’re back! How was home? Was it cold up there?
Really nice, thanks. I ate **way too much**, as usual. But it **wasn’t that cold**, which was strange. It’s **so much warmer than** when I was a kid. I was **in a T-shirt** most of the day.
In Đà Lạt? I didn’t expect that.
Yeah, my mum thinks it’s because they’ve built so much. Half the hills near our house **are covered in** greenhouses now.
That’s a bit sad. I still **picture it as** pine trees and fog.
Some parts are still like that. But the weekends are **really crowded** now. A lot of people **drive up** from Sài Gòn, and it’s hard to **find anywhere to park**.
To be fair, I was one of them last month.
Haha, that’s fine. **It’s good for business.** A few of my **old classmates** have **moved back** and opened coffee shops. Ten years ago, everyone was trying to leave.
That’s nice. Sài Gòn has changed a lot too. **It feels like a different city every few years.**
The metro, **for sure**. I used to spend an hour on my motorbike every morning, **stuck behind** buses. Now it takes about twenty minutes, and I can listen to podcasts on the way.
That’s a big improvement. Is there anything you don’t like?
They **turned** the market near my parents’ place **into** a shopping mall. It’s **handy**, I guess, but **it’s just not the same**. I used to go there with my grandma every Sunday.
**I get that.** It’s usually the small places you miss.

lesson.label: How has it changed?
head: Purposes
Phrases
rows:
• ***When I was a kid, it used to be…***
• ***Back then, there weren’t many…***
• ***I remember going to … with my family.***
• ***I used to spend a lot of time…***

• ***It’s a lot busier / bigger than it used to be.***
• ***There are a lot more … now.***
• ***They’ve built a new … near…***

• ***To be fair, some things have changed for the better.***
• ***It’s much easier to … now.***
• ***There’s a lot more to do now, like…***

• ***What I miss most is…***
• ***It’s more convenient now, but it’s not quite the same.***
• ***I sometimes miss how… it used to be.***
• ***I’m glad that … hasn’t changed.***

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. You may need to change the form of the verb.
homework.context: Linh and Khoa work at the same company in Hà Nội. Linh has been quiet all morning, so Khoa asks her about it at lunch.
lines: You’ve been quiet all morning. Everything OK?
Yeah, just thinking. My parents want me to {move back} to Hội An. My dad’s getting older, and they need help with the shop.
Oh. Do you want to go?
Part of me does. Living here really {wears you down}. I leave home at seven, get back at eight, and I’m always {stuck behind} a bus or a truck somewhere.
I know the feeling. But the {career prospects} here are much better. What would you do there?
That’s the problem. There aren’t many office jobs. But tourism is big now. Since the tourists started {pouring in}, new hotels and cafés have been {popping up} everywhere.
So you could probably find something.
Maybe. Our house is {a stone’s throw from} the river, so my mum wants to open a small homestay.
That sounds nice. Is the town still the same as when you were a kid?
The old town is. But the area around it has changed {beyond recognition}. My grandma’s rice fields are all hotels now.
{To be fair}, it’s given a lot of young people jobs. And people there still have a real {sense of community}. When my dad was in hospital last year, the neighbours took turns cooking for my mum.
You don’t get that here. I don’t even know my neighbours’ names.

homework.title: Part 2: Listening
homework.intro: Listen to Emma talking about her hometown, then do Parts A and B.

script.text: I grew up in Whitby, a small fishing town on the north-east coast of England. When I was a teenager, I couldn't wait to leave. ==There was one cinema, one bus to the city every two hours, and everyone knew your business.== So at eighteen, I moved to ==London== for university, and I ended up staying for twelve years.

Last spring, I went back for my brother's ==wedding==, and honestly, I was surprised. I expected the town to be exactly the same, but ==the harbour area was almost unrecognisable==. ==The old fish factory where my granddad worked has been turned into flats and a small brewery.== There were coffee shops on every corner, and most of the customers were tourists with cameras.

My first reaction was a bit negative. ==It felt like the town had lost something.== But then I talked to my old neighbour, Mrs Hall. She's lived there for seventy years, and I thought she'd complain. Instead, she said the changes were the best thing that had happened in a long time. ==Her grandchildren don't have to move away to find work anymore.== One of them runs a boat tour business.

Some things haven't changed, though. The fish and chips are still the best in the country, and I'm not just saying that. And people still stop to chat in the street. In London, I can go a whole week without talking to my neighbours.

So, would I move back? I've been thinking about it. ==House prices have gone up a lot, so it's not as cheap as it used to be. But I can work from home now, so finding a job isn't a problem.== Maybe in ==a couple of years==. For now, I'm just happy that I can see my hometown with fresh eyes.

options: She was offered a job in London.
She felt there was little to do and no privacy.
Her family decided to move to the city.
questions.why: “There was one cinema, one bus to the city every two hours, and everyone knew your business.”

questions.q: What surprised Emma when she went back?
options: The town looked exactly as she remembered.
The part of town near the sea had changed a lot.
There were fewer tourists than before.

questions.q: What happened to the place where her granddad worked?
options: It became a coffee shop for tourists.
It is now the office of a boat tour business.
It became homes and a place that makes beer.
questions.why: “The old fish factory… has been turned into flats and a small brewery.”

questions.q: How does Mrs Hall feel about the changes?
options: She thinks the town has become too crowded.
She is pleased because young people can stay in the town.
She complains that she no longer knows her neighbours.
questions.why: “Her grandchildren don’t have to move away to find work anymore.”

questions.q: Which sentence about Emma’s plans is TRUE?
options: She can’t move back because she would need a new job.
She has decided to move back next spring.
Houses cost more now, but working remotely makes moving back possible.
questions.why: “House prices have gone up a lot… But I can work from home now, so finding a job isn’t a problem.”

homework.title: Part 2B: Complete the summary
homework.instructions: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each blank.
homework.text: As a teenager, Emma found her hometown boring, so she left to study in {London}. Years later, she returned for a family {wedding} and found that the harbour was almost {unrecognisable|unrecognizable}. At first, she felt the town had {lost something}, but an elderly neighbour told her the changes were good, because young people no longer need to leave to find {work|jobs|a job}. Emma says the town is not as {cheap} as it used to be, but she may move back in {two years|2 years|a few years}.
